rv.q: There is an intoxicating quality of eloquent stillness to Jonathan Butterell’s production of Ashley Robinson’s play (his debut, incidentally, which is quite some way to start).
This is a gem of a show, marrying two arthouse-cool American actors with an oddball selection of offstage talent to produce something quietly moving.
The score gently expands what we see on stage: an achingly sad love story told with tenderness and care.
The men’s unlived lives, their unspent passions, are desolately evoked.
The effect is of a fine elegy but one without risk.
The piece packs a punch but it could and should leave you too floored to move.
Robinson’s play struggles to muster the scale, sweep and ultimately the tragic force that this love story demands; still, it is a finely drawn musical miniature of quiet compulsion.
But ultimately it isn’t enough to help the play step out of the film’s all-encompassing shadow.
It's a well-acted show but it's stagebound.
So, yes, it was brave to take on Brokeback Mountain, but I was left wondering why this new version needed to exist.
This is a piece in which absences strike you just as much as what’s present.

The story is sensitively handled and the overall result, beautiful and heartbreaking — a testament to the quality of the original source material and all those who’ve contributed their talents in bringing it to life.
This production worked on every level for me.
In short, Brokeback Mountain is a powerful and enticing production - the kind that tugs on your heartstrings with its sincerity.
The bare bones of the narrative are there; the dramatically necessary flesh and blood and sinew are not.
Where this new version of Brokeback Mountain struggles is in finding a way to let the emotion penned within the story fly; it feels confined in feeling, not in action.
The presence of these costumed musicians diminishes the rawness and immediacy of the drama and makes it feel like a civic exhibition staged for a crowd of yawning aldermen in a town hall.
But any emotions this production engenders around the topic are more likely earned by the audience’s memories of the source material rather than from the well-intentioned work on the stage.
Instead, what we witness is an artistically conservative and emotionally inert replay of prior material.
Utterly fantastic on every level, Brokeback Mountain is a masterpiece.
The story is a modern classic, and it is presented to perfection here.
Brokeback Mountain excels in unapologetically embracing the intimacy, passion and tactility of Jack and Ennis’ connection, which ultimately makes it all the more heartbreaking.

Step out of the auditorium and you realise you’ve just witnessed something very special indeed, as an audience we’ve been welcomed in to watch a delicate tale of forbidden love, and one that brings with it an expressive and stirring soundtrack.
Robinson makes his playwriting debut with this poignant 90-minute adaptation of her stand-out tale, Brokeback Mountain.

The audience encircles the central acting area which is surrounded by arid soil, and a campfire is alight. A band to one side plays illuminating country and western ballads sung by Eddi Reader whose throaty vocals recall Lucinda Williams.
All in all, Jonathan Butterell’s Brokeback Mountain doesn’t disappoint.
On the one hand, it’s lightweight, and too stifled to be boring.
Brokeback Mountain is a real masterpiece that's not to be missed. Simply put, this is a beautiful piece of theatre and is perhaps the easiest 5 star rating I've ever given to a play.
The production functions flawlessly and with enticing theatricality.
Where it could have been crass and queer-baity, this is in fact a delightfully nuanced, sensual and thought-provoking watch.

cn.t: Critics praise the intimate performances of Mike Faist and Lucas Hedges in this faithful stage adaptation, but many find the production struggles without the film's sweeping vistas, resulting in a sincere yet uneven chamber piece.

vr.q: Brokeback Mountain is a terrifically written well-acted play let down by the production
Ultimately it's not particularly satisfying and not particularly interesting.
